segments.text: Gentlemen, our session is going to be held in English and French. Please get your translators ready. Without any waste of time, I'm going to request, I'm going to ask some questions to the panels.

So we're just going to start by digging in. Madam Bendem, how does the current International Nuclear Society Council regional structure reflect today's global nuclear landscape? And in this context, how could a restructuring introduce an African region to better reorganize Africa's growing role while preserving existing member presentation and institutional balance? Thank you very much, Chair. So, I'm going to try to present in French.
It's more comfortable. So, the global professional networks are not just spaces for discussion. They are real accelerators for implementation.

So, I'm going to present to you first the current structure of the International Nuclear Society Council. We are a network of experts that brings together more than 80,000 experts at the global level in the areas of safety, security, safeguard, in all areas related to nuclear. So, we have a status of observer with the International Atomic Energy Agency and the United Nations Environment Program.

Our current structure, it brings together five regions, North America, Europe. So, we have the European Nuclear Society that brings together more than 30 national societies. So, we also have Latin America, South America, the Pan-Asian region.

This structure does not reflect the global situation that we want. So, we decided to add two regions, the African region and the At-Large region. So, as a Moroccan and as an African, under my leadership, during my mandate, I want to create the African Nuclear Society.

So, it will be officially launched during the next General Conference of the EU. And the At-Large region, which will bring together international organizations. For the moment, we have Women in Nuclear Global, which is already in this region, At-Large.

And we have discussed with the different managers, I hope that the IEA, the WNE, the OECD and NNM, why not, that they will be members of our board as At-Large members. So, each region brings precise expertise in several areas, in particular in the field of development of human competencies, the regulatory framework, the safety culture, the communication and engagement of the public, the deployment of technologies and innovation. So, Africa does not need to start from scratch.

It can draw from several decades of experience accumulated around the world. So, the network allows the development of capacities through mentoring programs, technical exchanges, joint training, academic partnerships, development of leadership. So, the strengthening of capacities does not only concern engineers and scientists, but also regulatory authorities, communicators, political decision-makers and industries.

So, if so, my vision is to create a real African nuclear ecosystem where knowledge, expertise and opportunities circulate beyond borders. So, my key message is to move from strengthening capacities to multiplying capacities through global collaboration. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Madam Bendam. Professional bodies are very important in terms of ensuring that there is collaboration and coordination across the professional areas. As a follow-up question, what role can professional networks play in harmonizing the safety culture and technical standards across African nuclear programs? Thank you very much.
It's a relevant question. The key points will be, mainly, the safety culture, which constitutes the foundation of any nuclear program. So, it must be the foundation.

So, technologies can be different, but safety principles must be and must remain universal. So, we must have different technologies, but the principles must be the same. So, professional networks create a dialogue between experts, regulatory authorities, exploiters, academic institutions, and decision-makers.

So, harmonization does not mean that we have the same ecosystem. On the other hand, we don't necessarily need to have identical systems. It consists of aligning common principles, shared standards, good practices, and a common vision of excellence in safety.

So, networks can support this goal through regional workshops, expert missions, and we often do this, either expert missions in Africa or in other European countries, shared standards, good practices, and a common vision of excellence in safety. So, networks can support this safety goal through, as I said, other than expert missions, we can have mentoring mechanisms between countries. So, countries with more advanced programs can support those who are just starting out.

That's why, as I said earlier, Africa does not have to invent everything. They can benefit from the advanced experience of other countries. So, safety culture does not only concern procedures, but it also relies on people, behavior, and collective responsibility.

Thank you. Thank you so much. We've already learned through these few days that key areas for the nuclear programs would be project financing and workforce development, and I'm happy that what you are sharing with us today is that your professional bodies play a key role in terms of workforce development.

Thank you so much for sharing generously with us. Engineer James Karari-Wahoko, tell us, within the East African Power Pool's competitive market structures, how can nuclear power be effectively integrated as a baseload resource whilst maintaining efficiencies and price stability? Whilst you're there, just indicate to us how you believe that the regional planning can be strengthened to incorporate nuclear energy as a shared capacity option aligned with nationally integrated resource plans. Thanks very much, Madam Moderator.

Just as an introduction, the EAPP is an organization of 13 countries, and it was formed back in 2005 with an objective of integrating the national power grids of these 13 member countries. So far, I think 11 out of the 13 are interconnected, at least with their neighbor. With the ultimate objective of promoting cross-border power trade, lowering electricity costs, and optimizing resource sharing, thereby improving grid stability and availability and access of electricity.

With regard to the trading that we currently have, it's based on bilateral contracts between our member countries. However, we are in the process of creating a competitive market. So where do we see nuclear playing in that space? Nuclear energy or nuclear power plants, as you all know, have high capital costs and long life.

And they would be best supported by long-term properties agreements rather than short-term power markets, which are volatile. However, in the long term, after the capital costs have been recovered, their cost of running are very marginal, are very small. Short-term costs.

And therefore, they can be competitive in the day-to-day market compared to other sources of electricity, including renewables. With regard to planning, each country does what is called its National Power System Master Plan or Integrated Resource Plan. And then at the regional level, what the EAPP does is to aggregate these national plans and look at ways of optimizing the regional resources and recommending ways of having an interconnected grid through transmission networks.
This is what we are currently doing. We have received support from the African Development Bank. We've just commissioned a study to undertake the Regional Power System Master Plan.

And we expect, once completed, it will include nuclear power projects, whether they're SMRs or conventional, as long as our member countries have included them in their plans. Ultimately, we expect that the Regional Power System Master Plan will be a consideration for the continental master plans, which hopes to have an integration of the five power pools of Africa, which are the Southern African Power Pool, Eastern Central African Power Pool, West African and North African Power Pool. With regard to scale, we see by 2028, we'll have the Southern African Power Pool and the Eastern African Power Pool interconnected, which creates a large scale of demand and supply, which makes it easier for nuclear power integration.
However, there still requires a lot of work to be done on the interconnectors. I think I'll stop there for the moment. Thank you so much.

And I think from what you're saying is that whilst we rally around building new generation capacity, we cannot ignore strengthening the grids. And I'm glad that you're mentioning the whole issue around the interconnected grids across the continent. And I think that's going to be crucial as well.

Thank you so much. Let's hear from you, Dr. Kofi Kofi. How can the West African Economic and Monetary Union support regional financing mechanisms to enable nuclear projects that serve multiple member states? And what role can regional economic blocks play in aggregating electricity demand to justify large scale nuclear investments? I would like to introduce my predecessors.

We have eight countries that are part of this economic and monetary organization. These are Benin, Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast, Guinea-Bissau, Mali, Niger, Senegal and Togo. And I would like to greet their representatives who are probably in the room, who have made the trip, and say that the population of the area is 10% of the African population.
We are about 140 million people. And we also have energy access up to 51%. And we have an energy production capacity of nearly 7 gigawatts per year.

And with that, we have, as I said, 51% of the total energy access. So you can see that today we have the issue of nuclear energy. So with this level, we have disparities that are important between countries.

So the need to develop nuclear energy has arrived at a certain point. But we already have a device that allows us to address the issue, since we have a market, a regional energy space. And furthermore, we even have all the energy networks of the sub-region that are interconnected, which will promote the exploitation of nuclear energy.

So at this level, what are the methods or financing possibilities and what can the Commission do? We have three ways in which we can work. First, there is the political dimension. You know that the sub-regional organization is first of all a political body that allows States to share common visions and to have coherent and harmonized approaches when there are decisions and actions to be taken.

Then you have the regulatory dimension on which we are going to work. We have begun to reflect because at the UN level, we are now taking community policies and this is very important. And on the aspect of direct financing, we have a financial market and I think that the opportunity of nuclear energy can raise funds, in particular bonds and obligations on the financial market.

This is quite possible and the Commission can support this in the case of nuclear projects and programs. So to go further on the second part that you touched on, what can the CEA do? Already at the level of the regional commission of the UN, we have a common energy program. We have a strategy of energy development that is based on the exploitation of all the energy potential that was adopted in 2023.

I remind you that we have a policy that was older, since 1999, but that has been revised on this occasion. And we are working together with all States and this policy is followed. We have launched a resource mobilization of about 10 billion dollars three years ago and things are going quite well.

So for nuclear energy, the Commission has been mandated to be able to reflect on the issue. Two years ago we were even here in Tigali with the board of Rwanda on nuclear energy. I would like to greet by the way Prime Minister Erbo who allowed us to be here and again invited us this time with the government of Rwanda.

So they did a job for us to identify the reference terms for a feasibility study and it will be done. And today I can tell you that the Commission will probably ask the organization of a summit of the heads of state of the sub-region. It is a file that will probably be registered at the next summit so that we have a political support a political support as part of an additional act so that we can work together.

Because there are some countries already in the sub-region three, I don't want to name them systematically that already have memorandums of cooperation with some partners and we wish that we can go together. The Minister said it, it was said yesterday. Together we succeed.

It is true that only there is the sovereignty of the states but we insist Madam that we go together through the Regional Commission and that is what we are doing. Thank you. Thank you, thank you so much and thank you so much for sharing the progress that is made through the economic blocks as well.

Ms. Demboyo, what strategic actions are required to achieve regulatory harmonization across African nuclear programs and how can the African Commission on Nuclear Energy strengthen coordination among member states to support shared infrastructure such as fuel cycle services or waste management facilities. Thank you. Thank you very much Madam Moderator for the two questions that you have directed toward me.

First of all I wanted to bring to your attention that the African Commission on Nuclear Energy which is the African body in charge of nuclear issues is continually encouraging African states on this journey of nuclear energy because development cannot stand if we don't have energy. We have over 600 million people all around Africa who lack energy because we cannot work on school issues, commercial issues, infrastructure without this key element. But on the issues of regulatory harmonization it can be achieved through establishment of mutual recognition agreements through joint assessment and inspections of nuclear power programs.

AFCON encourages and helps African states in order to come together on joint activities that we also organize. We bring them also together so that we can bring an harmony on this issue. The ideal is that we will, I mean those state parties, I mean those African countries, can deliver, I mean reach the development goals in a safe manner.

So in coherency together so we offer also those opportunities. On the other side regarding the fuel cycle and waste management infrastructure shared ones as you have said, the African states can use Palindaba Treaty to harmonize nuclear regulations and establish continental capacity building framework and pool resources together to implement shared fuel cycle and waste management infrastructure among others. Also the Palindaba Treaty itself, its framework can be used to regional infrastructure and joint benefit.
Share the fuel cycle and radioactive storage facilities to avoid duplication costs and others. So this is a key or brief answer that I can provide for these questions. Thank you Madam.

Thank you so much Mr. Mboyo for your inputs. Let's hear from engineer Felchesmi Mramba from the Minister of Energy Tanzania. How can regional energy cooperation within East Africa support Tanzania's long-term strategy for integrating nuclear energy into a secure and diversified energy mix? And what strategic investments are most critical to ensure that nuclear deployment contributes not only to the energy security but also to regional industrialization and economic transformation? Thank you so much and let me build on the foundation which was made by Minister Mboyo and my good friend here.

He spoke about the advantages of collaboration especially within the East African community as well as the Southern African community. Tanzania as it was communicated to the citizens the first day of this meeting has ambitions for developing nuclear energy and we understand that to be able to do whatever we are planning we need to operate within the community of collaborating countries. Now, number one, one of the advantages we may take being members of East African community is for example taking advantage of the existing collaboration infrastructures or rather structures like the Eastern African Power Pool where we believe that when you belong in a pool you have an advantage of a big market but again you have a big pool of expertise and without forgetting the advantage of interconnectivity among the countries.

For example, right now Tanzania is interconnected with Kenya at a 400kv transmission line. We are again interconnected with Burundi and Rwanda through Sumo at 220kv and we have started constructing another line interconnecting Tanzania and Zambia and soon we are going to start a new project interconnecting Tanzania and Uganda both at 400kv. Now, these interconnections are giving us advantage that when we have nuclear power within the country we are already interconnected within the region which gives us advantage in terms of the market in terms of sharing different resources like my colleague here was speaking about sharing disposal of the waste and the other options and at the same time developing nuclear infrastructure which does not go as a standalone project.

It is the whole ecosystem and here we are talking of other investments like human capital that we need to start building human capital, investing on people and we are again looking at how we can start looking for utilisation of the power we are going to generate and we believe this should go hand in hand with policies, for example industrial policies which will ensure that once you generate a huge amount of power from nuclear, you also have policies on how to absorb the power you are generating, whether it is cross-border trading, whether it is industrial zones where this power will be utilised or whether it is within the power pools where the generated power will be utilised. Thank you so much. It is very encouraging to hear about the progress that is being made in terms of looking at interconnectivity because it is going to be very crucial as we start with these big projects that we are anticipating.

Madam Bendam, I would like to find out from you how can knowledge-sharing platforms be leveraged to reduce deployment risks and shorten project timelines? Thank you very much, Cher. One of the biggest deployment risks is a repeating challenge already solved ever here. I can give you some examples.

My area of expertise is CPR, emergency preparedness and response. The IEA published different reports on different accidents in order not that we repeat the same problems. Also, about knowledge-sharing platforms.

I remember in 2015 we organised the first radiological exercise for English-speaking countries in Botswana. I had the chance to prepare this exercise, conduct it and evaluate it for English-speaking countries. In 2015, we organised another exercise.

Also, it's the first exercise for French-speaking countries in Senegal in 2018. The idea is to speak about knowledge-sharing. Each exercise in general takes more than between six months until one year of preparation.

When we speak about preparation, we should prepare the exercise manual, control manual, evaluate manual, a lot of work. The idea, when we organised this exercise at a regional level, after I shared this document with African countries and just adapt the scenario and they can prepare their own exercise and they will not have a lot of time to prepare this exercise. The idea that when we share knowledge, we save time, we save money, we save a lot of things.

Now, I can explain that new nuclear programs often face similar challenges. So, regularity development, infrastructure readiness, workforce development or financing approach. Knowledge-sharing platforms provide access to listen and learn, good practice.
When I speak about listen and learn, this is what the IEA in general share in example, the reports. This is because EPR is my area of expertise. That's why I give this example.

So, knowledge-sharing platforms also provide access to technical repositories, technical studies, case studies, and also real-time collaboration. So, they help to identify challenges early before they become delayed and finally, learning from previous experience reduces first-of-kind risk, uncertainty, and duplication of efforts. So, digital platforms combined with the strong professional network can create continent-wide knowledge ecosystem.
So, the goal is not simply to share information, but to transfer knowledge into action. Thank you. Thank you so much.

I think usually when we talk about knowledge-sharing, it's always easier said than done. I'm glad that you are mentioning that platforms are being created. I think what's key is to make sure that when we've got these platforms that have got a repository of a lot of information, we need to ensure access in terms of people accessing it so that they can start gaining the knowledge.

Thank you so much, Madam, for sharing that. Engineer Wahoko, what are the priority investments and coordination mechanisms that are required to ensure grid stability and reliability for integrating large-scale nuclear capacity across the region? Thanks very much for that question. At EAPP, we have to ensure that the grid is operating in a stable manner, in a secure manner, and given that we are having many countries getting interconnected, we must ensure that they comply with what we call our interconnection code.

So what we have done over the last one or two years is to undertake a study and model the power system across the countries which are interconnected, and we have developed what we call control areas. These are areas who will be managing the control over the large interconnected system and their jurisdictions. And then we have also developed an investment plan for the member utilities to implement to ensure that the grid is stable, not just for nuclear energy, but for all power projects, including renewable energy generators and the transmission system interconnections.
So this work has been completed, and it is ongoing. So we expect the next phase will be for the member countries to implement the investment plan. Thank you so much.

That is good progress. Dr. Kofi Kofi, how can the West African Economic and Monetary Union align energy policies among member states to support coordinated nuclear deployments? We have realistic and the different constraints, opportunities, advantages and risks are taken into account. This is absolutely necessary.

It gives guarantees to states. It gives guarantees and assurances to partners, investors, but also to the population. This morning we followed the issue of confidence in the population because there is always a fear that nuclear energy is dangerous.
This idea is not strong because there are past experiences that everyone knows in the world. So we have to reassure the population. They have to participate in these initiatives.

Let's not forget that we have to work in the long run. We often have difficulties when there is political These are projects that have to stay in the long run so that a coming government does not question the initiatives taken by its predecessor. Let's not forget that there are also emergencies in the states.
We must not neglect them. We need this. We need this coalition, the regional space.
It is not excluded. I think these are things that we are studying. A regional authority will manage these issues and harmonize the regulations because we are not going to the unknown.

If we have to leave 8 countries each to lead their regulations, we will have difficulties because they are elements of guarantee, investments, and see all the fiscal aspects, regulatory aspects, financial aspects, in fact all the aspects of human capital. We need to have people, engineers, people who are able to manage the equipment and the products, investments, without forgetting that we have a technology to learn from abroad. We have to make sure that even if they are difficult, we put the key under the umbrella.
We have seen many projects that have been left without a sequel because we don't have the code. To put a little humor, we don't have the code of the project. This is very important.
This is what we are going to do in the coming months, lead this work well and also this elaboration of a community regulation. Thank you. Thank you so much.

I am also pleased to also hear you mentioning the whole issue around creating awareness and also making sure that we demystify the fear for nuclear. I was so impressed in the last few weeks that we ran a competition as the BRICS Nuclear Platform Atoms Empowering Africa which was open to young people. We had a lot of applications and we adjudicated over 36 applications.

I was impressed with the fact that a lot of us, the senior citizens, we worried about the young people who are afraid of nuclear. But what I saw from the projects, I know that it is promising for Africa. Thank you so much.

Mr. Mboyo, what role should the African Commission on Nuclear Energy play in reinforcing governance frameworks to build long-term investment confidence and support Africa's nuclear agenda? Thank you very much Madam Moderator. This issue of investment is capital, because it is very important and key. Regarding resource mobilization, AFCON facilitates partnership to help member states secure international funding and technical assistance.
We often do that to help in the maximum partnership so that this can be secured. This is the answer I can give on this. Thank you so much.

Let's hear from Njiniem Ramba. What role should governance play in translating regional political commitments into coordinated implementation frameworks for large-scale energy infrastructure projects such as nuclear power? Governments have a lot of roles to play. Here we are talking of regional collaborations.

We are talking of involvement of private sector. But when it comes to governments, here we are talking of establishment of institutional and regulatory framework which will ensure that whatever investment we are doing on nuclear energy is properly managed, but there is a regulation, there are institutions which are established to manage the investments we are putting together. But again, we are looking at coordination of different institutions, different parties which will make our investment and the whole program on nuclear energy feasible.

Governance will be very important and governments are responsible to see that they bring together, they put together policies, they establish regulatory frameworks, they put together institutions which are capable of supervising and managing the investments we are putting. Thank you. Thank you so much.

I think just to come back to the panel, your final parting words given that the scale and capital intensity of nuclear projects is a concern. What do you propose that African countries can do to collaborate to create regional financing platforms and risk sharing mechanisms that make nuclear deployment bankable and attractive to the private sector? One idea. Let's start with you, madam.
One idea? Yes, one idea. Establish risk sharing mechanisms to reassure private It's an idea. Establish risk sharing mechanisms to reassure private investors.
And multiply, mutualize financing through regional African and development banks. Thank you. Thank you so much.

One idea each. I think for me the example I would give is perhaps to copy and replicate what has been done by Rwanda, Burundi and Tanzania in the development of Rosumo Falls, because the three countries have jointly done a generation plant. That can be replicated also into developing a nuclear plant as well.
Thank you. Dr. Kofi Kofi? One idea. Okay.
To go together is better than to go each by each. Thank you so much. Thank you very much, Madam Moderator.
And thank you for my colleague here to go together. So that's fantastic. The African state can collaborate to make nuclear deployment bankable by establishing regional nuclear energy consortium.

The Palindaba Treaty can be used to establish this mechanism. Pooling of capital resources can allow African states to share the heavy upfront costs and other expenditures. And then African states can also implement cross border risk sharing mechanisms, of course.
This is because nuclear projects carry long term political construction and demand risk. So this is the view on that. Thank you.

For me, number one, African countries must be able to join together and show to the investors that we have a big market. Big markets are only available when we interconnect our countries. I come to the need for interconnections between countries with transmission lines and power infrastructure.

That will help to create a big market and once you have a big market, you attract more investments and different parties will be attracted to that market. But finally, I'm looking at collaboration in terms of creating pool of expertise, but again countries collaborating together to put together standards and grid codes which will make all these investments be able to operate within a bigger region. Thank you.

Thank you so much. Ladies and gentlemen, we've had the pleasure of listening and engaging with our esteemed panelists here. And for me, I think the take home is that we need to build together, we need to build trust, we need to copy and replicate where there's been progress.

There are frameworks that are in place like your Pelendaba Treaty, let's use them and let's work together. Africa's pursuit of energy security and sustainable future increasingly includes nuclear and we cannot ignore that. Achieving this ambition, however, depends not only on infrastructure and technology but developing a strong, skilled and future-oriented workforce across the continent.
I think the organizers owe us coffee, we have managed to say five minutes, so thank you so much to the panel. Please let's appreciate them. Thank you so much.
Let's appreciate Elsie and her team. Guys, let's appreciate the panel.

parts.title: Hon. Dr. Jimmy Gasore, Minister of Infrastructure

segments.text: Distinguished delegates, leaders of international institutions, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

It is indeed a privilege and honour to address this distinguished gathering at a moment when Africa is redefining its energy future and strengthening its collective ambitions for industrial transformation, economic resilience and sustainable development. I commend the organisers for convening this important plenary on regional cooperation and deployment at scale, a subject that goes to the heart of Africa's development agenda. Today, Africa faces both a challenge and an opportunity of historic proportions.

Our continent is home to more than 1.4 billion people, and by 2050, one in every four people in the world will be African. Africa's economy is expanding, urbanisation is accelerating and our young population is driving unprecedented demand for energy, industry, mobility and digital infrastructure and manufacturing. Distinguished delegates, the success of the African continent free trade area will depend heavily on Africa's ability to provide reliable and affordable energy at scale.

The AFCFTA represents a market of more than 1.4 billion people with a combined GDP exceeding 3.4 trillion US dollars. It has the potential to increase intra-African trade by more than 50% and significantly expand regional manufacturing and industrial value chains. But industrialisation cannot happen in the dark.

Factories cannot operate competitively without stable electricity and digital economies cannot thrive without reliable power systems. Regional trade cannot expand without an integrated infrastructure. This is why Africa's energy transition must also become a regional integration project.

Nuclear energy is increasingly emerging as a part of Africa's long-term energy strategy because it offers three critical advantages. One, it provides reliable baseload electricity to support industrial economies. Second, it offers low carbon generation essential for climate resilience and sustainable growth.

And lastly, it strengthens long-term energy security by diversifying national and regional energy systems. However, nuclear deployment requires significant investment, advanced regulatory systems, highly specialised expertise and long-term infrastructure planning. Distinguished delegates, the priority must be regional market aggregation.

Individually, many African energy markets are relatively small. But collectively, Africa represents one of the world's largest emerging energy opportunities. Regional power integration can create economies of scale, improve project bankability and reduce electricity costs, and attract long-term infrastructure financing.

Already, regional power systems or regional power pools, such as the East African Power Pool, the Southern African Power Pool, as well as the West African Power Pool, are demonstrating the strategic value of interconnected electricity markets. Africa must continue investing in cross-border transmission infrastructure, integrated grid systems and regional energy trade mechanisms capable of supporting large-scale deployment of clean energy technologies. The other thing we must strengthen is regulatory alignment across the continent.

For a nuclear energy to succeed, investors and citizens alike must have confidence in safety, transparency and governance. Africa, therefore, needs a stronger cooperation in regulatory capacity building, licensing framework, nuclear safety standards and technical oversight. Our experience has shown that collaboration accelerates progress.

Whether through regional power interconnections, clean energy partnerships, digital innovations or infrastructure integration, Africa advances faster when it acts together. Africa now has a historic opportunity: a young population, a continental free trade area, a rapidly growing market and expanding regional institutions. This is an urgent global transition toward clean systems.

All of those create opportunities for our continent. The decisions we make today will determine whether Africa becomes merely a consumer in the global energy transition or a strategic leader within it. The future we seek requires courage, coordination and long-term vision.

It requires us to move beyond fragmented planning toward continental ambitions. It requires us to build energy systems that power industries, create jobs, support trade, strengthen resilience and improve the lives of our citizens. Above all, it requires us to recognize that Africa's greatest strength is not the size of individual markets but the power of our collective action.
Together, Africa can build an integrated, secure and sustainable energy future capable of powering prosperity for generations to come. I thank you very much for your kind attention.
